guidance: Paste a pattern the way you would after bazel build. The working directory is the package Bazel would start from, not the workspace root, so it only changes relative patterns.
method: The pattern is read with the label grammar from Bazel's label documentation and the target-pattern table from the commands documentation. An optional leading - subtracts the pattern from the ones before it. The repository part is optional: @name// is an apparent repository, @@name// a canonical one, and @@// always means the main repository, even from an external one; a repository name cannot contain a space, slash, colon or @. The package is the path between // and the first colon, and the target is what follows; a colon inside the target is refused. With no colon the last path segment becomes the target, so //my/app means //my/app:app rather than the package my/app, and //foo/bar/wiz always means //foo/bar/wiz:wiz even when no such package exists. Package names are ASCII and are limited to letters, digits and Bazel's punctuation set: no colon, no tilde, no //, no leading or trailing slash, and no . or .. segment. A target may contain non-ASCII characters and slashes, but a slashed target must be a normal relative path: no leading, trailing or doubled slash and no . or .. segment. The ... wildcard must be the last package segment and selects whole packages; it is expanded to :all, or to :* or :all-targets, which also match files and implicit outputs such as _deploy.jar. Targets tagged manual are skipped by build and test wildcards but not by bazel query. A relative pattern is resolved against the working directory. A relative path with a slash and no colon is genuinely ambiguous, because only the BUILD files decide whether the full path or its parent is a package, so all three readings are listed instead of one being guessed. The page reads no BUILD files and contacts no build server; it normalizes and explains the spelling, and cannot prove that a package or target exists.
